summary:
ASTRA is an integrated astronaut health intelligence platform designed to help crews monitor, understand, and protect their health during space missions. It combines seven health domains—immune, musculoskeletal, sleep and recovery, mental and behavioral, cardiovascular and respiratory, cognitive and functional, and nutrition and metabolism—with mission and environmental data, including radiation, microgravity, spacecraft conditions, circadian disruption, and operational stressors.

Through an interactive dashboard, ASTRA aims to present health indicators, track changes over time, highlight measurements that may require attention, and provide accessible guidance on preventive actions and health improvements, supporting astronauts and communication with flight surgeons without replacing professional medical judgment.

Its Research Lab connects health observations with spaceflight exposures and molecular evidence, using publicly available datasets such as NASA’s Open Science Data Repository, NASA Eyes on the Solar System, NASA Integrated Medical Model (IMM) and more to investigate potential biological mechanisms and health risks. By integrating health monitoring, mission context, and scientific research, ASTRA seeks to support earlier awareness, evidence-based decisions, and safer, more sustainable human space exploration.
details:
ASTRA is an integrated astronaut health intelligence platform designed to help crew members assess, monitor, understand, and protect their health during space missions. Its central concept is to connect three dimensions that are often analyzed separately: astronaut health, the spaceflight environment, and scientific research.

The platform is organized into interconnected modules:

1. Astronaut Health Assessment and Monitoring

ASTRA organizes health monitoring into seven domains:

  • Immune Health: T-cell and B-cell function, immune cell populations, cytokines, inflammatory biomarkers, and immune-related gene expression.
  • Musculoskeletal Health: Muscle strength, bone health, mobility, and physical capacity.
  • Sleep and Recovery: Sleep duration, quality, interruptions, and circadian rhythm.
  • Mental and Behavioral Health: Stress, perceived isolation, mood, and psychological well-being.
  • Cardiovascular and Respiratory Health: Heart rate, blood pressure, oxygenation, and cardiorespiratory capacity.
  • Cognitive and Functional Performance: Attention, memory, reaction time, coordination, and cognitive fatigue.
  • Nutrition and Metabolism: Nutritional intake, hydration, body composition, and metabolic indicators.

The planned Health Assessment experience includes an interactive human body map, guided assessments, symptom reporting, and multiple data-input methods, such as manual entries, compatible sensor measurements, questionnaires, and laboratory results. Each assessment is designed to explain what is being measured, why it matters, and how to perform it.

2. Health Insights and Preventive Guidance

ASTRA aims to transform health measurements into understandable information through visual indicators, longitudinal charts, historical comparisons, and configurable attention levels. It will help astronauts identify measurements that may require monitoring, verification, or escalation to the appropriate medical team.

The platform also aims to provide accessible explanations and preventive guidance based on validated medical protocols, including authorized exercise, sleep, hydration, and nutritional recommendations. ASTRA is not intended to replace flight surgeons or provide independent clinical diagnoses.

3. Mission Tracking and Space Environment Intelligence

ASTRA considers that astronaut health cannot be interpreted independently of mission conditions. This module is designed to integrate mission stages, trajectory information, and environmental exposures, including:

  • Space radiation, including galactic cosmic rays and solar particle events.
  • Microgravity, partial gravity, and gravity transitions.
  • Spacecraft habitat conditions, including oxygen, carbon dioxide, pressure, temperature, and humidity.
  • Light exposure, circadian disruption, and sleep schedules.
  • Isolation, confinement, workload, stress, nutrition, and exercise.

By organizing these factors alongside health observations, ASTRA provides a framework for investigating possible exposure–response relationships over time.

4. ASTRA Research Lab

The Research Lab connects astronaut health observations with publicly available space biology research and molecular evidence during the flight.

Using resources such as NASA's Open Science Data Repository (OSDR) and other data, ASTRA supports the exploration of longitudinal measurements, immune-related biomarkers, gene expression, cytokine signaling, inflammatory pathways, and other biological mechanisms.

Our initial research work uses publicly available Inspiration4 data, including Complete Blood Count (CBC), Comprehensive Metabolic Panel (CMP), and serum protein measurements. We have organized data from four participants across seven study timepoints and conducted preliminary comparisons and data-quality audits.

These audits identified records requiring further verification, including inconsistencies in a leukocyte differential, unusual hematological measurements, and protein or metabolic values that need additional assay and metadata review. These findings are treated as data-quality flags, not confirmed medical abnormalities or evidence of flight-induced disease.

This Research Lab aims to support evidence-based investigation while distinguishing observed associations from causal conclusions.

5. Data Integrity and Scientific Evidence

ASTRA distinguishes measured, historical, estimated, and simulated information. It is designed to preserve data sources, units, timestamps, missing values, measurement methods, uncertainty, and methodological limitations. This is essential for responsible interpretation of sensitive astronaut health information.

Benefits and Intended Impact

ASTRA seeks to make astronaut health information more accessible, understandable, and actionable. Its intended benefits include:

  • Supporting earlier awareness of potentially concerning health changes.
  • Helping astronauts understand health indicators and complete assessments correctly.
  • Encouraging preventive routines and consistent health monitoring.
  • Improving the interpretation of physiological changes in the context of mission exposures.
  • Connecting operational health monitoring with molecular and biological research.
  • Supporting communication and evidence-informed decisions between astronauts and medical teams.

Its long-term vision is to contribute to safer and more sustainable human exploration, particularly during extended missions to the Moon, Mars, and other demanding space environments.

AI, Tools and Technologies

The web prototype was developed using:

  • Next.js and React for the application structure and interface.
  • TypeScript for typed application development.
  • Tailwind CSS for responsive interface styling.
  • Lucide React for interface icons and visual elements.
  • Python for dataset inspection, comparison, and preliminary data-quality auditing.
  • Codex, Claude for design, coding, data analysis, debugging, and fixing errors
  • Copilot for coding, data analysis, and research

The current prototype uses historical research data, especially from Inspiration4, and conceptual mission visualizations as examples. It does not yet have a live astronaut telemetry connection or dedicated medical hardware integration. Sensor integration, image-based assessment, interactive body mapping, and advanced analytical capabilities are planned development areas.

Creativity and Design Considerations

ASTRA's creativity lies in combining an astronaut-centered health experience with an integrated scientific research environment. Rather than presenting isolated measurements, it seeks to connect what is happening to the astronaut, what conditions are present during the mission, and what biological mechanisms may help explain observed changes.

The project considers the practical limitations of space missions, including restricted medical resources, limited measurement opportunities, communication constraints, crew workload, and the need for clear instructions. It also considers usability, accessibility, data privacy, scientific reliability, and the importance of distinguishing medical guidance from exploratory research.

Ultimately, ASTRA aims to transform space health monitoring from a collection of separate measurements into an integrated system for understanding, tracking, and protecting human health beyond Earth.
